doc.title: Michael Max Fleming interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

chapter: Mary Lou Williams and learning by ear
title: Mary Lou Williams and Ben Webster: Body and Soul, use your ears
summary: His first big New York gig was with Mary Lou Williams at Wells. He declined to play Body and Soul for Ben Webster and was insulted. She then told him to use his ears.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: What happens as a bassist when you go to play a gig and maybe it’s a pick-up group or something, and someone calls a tune and you don’t know it. But you’re supposed to know it. You’re supposed to be responsible for outlining the changes. How do you get through that?

I got through that from one big experience from — I didn’t tell you but the first major gig that I got in after I moved to New York was with Mary Lou Williams — the liaison between the swing and the bebop. A lot of people don’t know it but she helped Monk form his sound, helped Bud Powell form their sounds. She was well respected. She’s my musical mother, and that’s within the first six weeks I got into her hands and her influence. So she’s coming out of retirement, she’s playing at Wells. Upstairs they had two bands. A lot of places had two bands. I’m upstairs and I come up off of a break one night and there’s this guy sitting there, an older gentleman. His name was Ben Webster. So I come up to him, “Good evening, sir.” All prim and proper. And in a way you’d say a country bumpkin, I don’t know, with a Midwestern accent. So I sounded like somebody from Chicago maybe. So, “What would you like to play?” talking to Ben Webster. “Body and Soul.” Now from my Cincinnati training there was a culture to that. If you couldn’t call the changes to the tune all the way through you don’t play that. “I’m sorry, could you play something else?” I’m telling you the culture with my uncle and the way they worked. So now I say that and a chill comes over the room. Because people sitting in are not really playing but they’re watching but I don’t know if it was because the expression changed on his face or whatever but I says, “I don’t know that but could you call another tune please?” But I get this response, didn’t come rapidly enough — oh I can’t say this —
It’s a word, it’s a dirty word.

So you know what he said to me? “You ain’t shit.” Now my uncle was also a street person and those are fighting words partner. So now thinking of my uncle, I’m saying, “Hmmm. I’ve got a rough customer here.” So according to my uncle, if you’re going to jump on somebody like that you orchestrate it, first you’re going to do just like a football.

That’s where he learned it from. First you snap the ball, then you make an end run, and then you fake. So which way am I going to whip this old man? So the voice came in my mind says, “Don’t do that, Michael because you know Charles Mingus’ got a bad reputation and you just got in town. Don’t you start a fight, you’ll never get work.” So whatever happened? I don’t remember what tune we played but we played something else and then I walked across the floor to Mary Lou Williams, who was sitting there. And she’s looking at me with this indefinable look. And I’m like a little kid coming to my mommy. And she looks at me and she says, “You ain’t shit. Man don’t you ever embarrass me like that. When you don’t know a tune use your ears.” You asked me about how I do what I do. Use your ears. That was 1963. On and off I played with her up until 1971 and even further than that. And during that time she gave me little hints of what you do. So when I come on the gig and somebody, “Do you know ‘S’wonderful’?” Yeah. If they ask me, “You know ‘S’wonderful’?” Yeah. Play it.
First time around — second time around got you. But she showed me. So does that answer you?
